title: Ultima vs Liquid IV: Which Electrolyte Mix Is Better?
excerpt: Ultima vs Liquid I.V. compared: sugar, sodium, potassium, and magnesium per serving, which helps more after drinking, which suits keto or daily use, and who should be careful.
metaDescription: Ultima vs Liquid IV: sugar, sodium, and minerals compared, which is better for a hangover or daily hydration, and who should check with a doctor first.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Ultima Replenisher and Liquid I.V. look like they're in the same category, but they're built for opposite people. Liquid I.V. is a sodium-forward hydration mix with a small dose of sugar, designed around the same salt-plus-glucose idea as a medical oral rehydration solution. Ultima is a zero-sugar, stevia-sweetened mix that's low in sodium and leans on potassium and magnesium instead. That makes Liquid I.V. the better tool when you're actually dried out, such as after a night of drinking, a hot day, or a stomach bug. Ultima is the better fit if you want something you can sip every day without sugar or much salt, or if a doctor has told you to watch your sodium. Neither one cures a hangover, because dehydration is only one piece of why you feel bad.

**The quick picks:**

- **Hangover morning, thirsty, headachy, mildly dried out:** Liquid I.V. (original), one stick in about 16 ounces of water.
- **Vomiting or diarrhea after drinking:** Liquid I.V. is closer to what you need, but a true oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte, DripDrop) is better still.
- **Everyday sipping, no sugar, low sodium:** Ultima.
- **Keto, low-carb, or managing blood sugar:** Ultima, or Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free if you want more sodium.
- **High blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or you take medicines that affect potassium:** talk to your doctor before using either regularly. Liquid I.V. carries more sodium; Ultima carries a fair amount of potassium and magnesium, which matter for kidney patients too.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares general label information and research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Formulas and flavors change, so check your own package for current numbers. **Get medical help instead of reaching for an electrolyte drink if** you can't keep fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood, you've barely urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle. If someone who drank heavily is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, that may be alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

## Ultima vs Liquid I.V. at a Glance

These are approximate figures for the standard versions at the time of writing. Both brands sell several product lines and adjust recipes over time, so treat this as a guide to the overall shape of each product, not exact label values.

| | Ultima Replenisher (standard) | Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier (original) |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | 0 g | Around 11 g (cane sugar and dextrose) |
| Calories | Close to zero | Around 45 |
| Sweetener | Stevia leaf extract | Sugar (Sugar-Free line uses allulose and other sweeteners) |
| Sodium | Low, roughly 50 to 60 mg | Around 500 mg |
| Potassium | Around 250 mg | Around 370 mg |
| Magnesium | Notable, roughly 100 mg | Not a significant source |
| Other minerals | Calcium, chloride, phosphate | Chloride (from salt) |
| Added vitamins | Vitamin C and zinc in some versions | Vitamin C and several B vitamins |
| Water per serving | About 16 fl oz (check your label) | About 16 fl oz |
| Taste | Light, lightly sweet, stevia finish | Sweet and salty, close to a sports drink |
| Marketed for | Everyday hydration, clean-label, keto | Fast hydration, travel, hangovers, heat |

The two lines that matter most are sodium and sugar. Liquid I.V. has roughly ten times the sodium of Ultima per serving. Ultima has no sugar at all. Those two differences decide which one makes sense for you, and the rest of this article explains why.

## Why Sodium and Sugar Decide the Matchup

Plain water is absorbed fine when you're healthy. When you're actually losing fluid, though, the body needs salt to hold on to the water it takes in. Sodium is the main mineral that keeps water in your bloodstream and in the space around your cells. Drink a lot of plain water when you're low on sodium and your kidneys simply pass much of it out again.

There's also a transport trick in your small intestine. A protein in the gut wall moves sodium and glucose into the body together, and water follows them. A drink with the right balance of sodium plus a little glucose is therefore absorbed more efficiently than either salt water or sugar water alone. This is the principle behind oral rehydration solution (ORS), which the World Health Organization and UNICEF have promoted for decades to treat dehydration from diarrheal illness. It's one of the best-supported treatments in public health.

Here's how the two brands line up against that principle:

- **Liquid I.V.** uses it directly. The brand calls its formula "Cellular Transport Technology," which is a marketing name for the same sodium-and-glucose idea. It has a meaningful amount of sodium and a modest amount of sugar.
- **Ultima** doesn't use it. With no glucose and very little sodium, it doesn't trigger that transport system. It adds minerals to your water and makes it taste better, which can help you drink more, but it doesn't pull water in the way an ORS does.

### Where each sits next to the WHO formula

The WHO's reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration salts contain about 75 mmol of sodium per liter, which is roughly 1,700 mg of sodium per liter, along with a small amount of glucose. Using the approximate label figures above:

- **Liquid I.V.** mixed in 16 ounces (about half a liter) works out to roughly 1,000 mg of sodium per liter. That's below a medical ORS but in the same general neighborhood.
- **Ultima** mixed in 16 ounces works out to roughly 100 to 120 mg of sodium per liter. That's a small fraction of the ORS level, closer to a mineral water than a rehydration drink.

That gap is the single most important thing to understand about this comparison. Ultima isn't a weaker Liquid I.V. It's a different kind of product.

## Ultima Replenisher: What It Is and Who It's For

Ultima Replenisher is a powdered electrolyte mix that has been sold in the US since the 1990s. It comes in stick packs, larger tubs, and a few newer formats. Its pitch is a "clean" hydration drink: zero sugar, sweetened with stevia, no artificial colors or flavors, and suitable for vegan and keto diets. Instead of relying on sodium, it spreads a smaller dose across several minerals, usually listed as six electrolytes: sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, chloride, and phosphate.

**What it does well:**

- **No sugar, almost no calories.** Good if you're managing blood sugar, eating low-carb, or simply don't want sugar in a drink you have every day.
- **Low sodium.** A genuine plus if you've been told to limit salt, or if you already eat a salty diet and just want flavored water.
- **Magnesium and potassium.** Many people don't get enough of either from food. A daily serving adds a useful amount of both.
- **Easy to drink.** The flavor is light, which helps some people drink more water through the day than they would plain.

**Where it falls short:**

- **Not built for real dehydration.** With very little sodium and no glucose, it doesn't do what an oral rehydration solution does. After vomiting, diarrhea, or heavy sweating, it won't replace the sodium you lost.
- **Stevia aftertaste.** Some people love it; others find it bitter or "diet" tasting.
- **The magnesium can loosen stools.** Magnesium citrate in larger amounts has a mild laxative effect. One serving is unlikely to bother most people, but several servings on a morning when alcohol has already upset your gut could make diarrhea worse.
- **Potassium matters for some people.** For most healthy adults it's a benefit. For people with kidney disease or who take medicines that raise potassium, it's something to check with a doctor.

## Liquid I.V.: What It Is and Who It's For

Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier is one of the best-known hydration mixes in the US. A stick goes into about 16 ounces of water and adds around 500 mg of sodium, around 370 mg of potassium, a small amount of cane sugar and dextrose, and vitamin C plus several B vitamins. It also sells Sugar-Free, Energy (with caffeine), and Sleep (with melatonin and other ingredients) lines. For a deeper look at the brand on its own, see our full guide to [Liquid I.V. for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover).

**What it does well:**

- **Follows rehydration science.** The sodium-plus-glucose formula is the right shape for replacing fluid you've actually lost.
- **Enough sodium to make a difference.** After a night of drinking, sweating, or a long flight, that sodium helps your body keep the water you drink.
- **Familiar taste.** Most people find it sweet and easy to finish, more like a sports drink than a medicine.
- **Widely available.** You can find it at most grocery stores, pharmacies, and big-box stores.

**Where it falls short:**

- **Sugar.** About 11 g per stick is modest, but it adds up if you have it daily, and it's not ideal for people managing diabetes. The Sugar-Free version fixes this but gives up some of the glucose-driven absorption benefit.
- **Sodium load.** Around 500 mg per stick is a real chunk of the daily limit many health bodies recommend. Two or three sticks a day on top of a normal diet is a lot of salt.
- **Not a full ORS.** For serious dehydration from illness, a purpose-built oral rehydration solution is a better match. Our [DripDrop vs Liquid I.V. comparison](/never-hungover/drip-drop-vs-liquid-iv) covers that difference in detail.

## Ultima vs Liquid I.V. for a Hangover

If you're choosing between these two the morning after drinking, Liquid I.V. is the more useful option for most people. Here's why.

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink. It does this by lowering a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of that signal, more fluid leaves your body, and some sodium and potassium go with it. Add sweating in a warm bar, a short night of sleep, and maybe some vomiting or diarrhea, and you can wake up genuinely low on fluid and salt.

Liquid I.V. is designed to replace exactly that: water plus sodium, with a little glucose to help absorption. Ultima mostly adds water and flavor, with a light sprinkle of minerals. If plain water helps you on a hangover morning, Ultima will help about as much as plain water, maybe a little more if the flavor gets you to drink more of it. Liquid I.V. has a better chance of actually restoring fluid balance.

That said, keep expectations realistic. Hangover researchers have found that how dehydrated people are doesn't line up neatly with how bad their hangover feels. The headache, fatigue, nausea, and low mood come mostly from other things: poor-quality sleep, inflammation, acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), stomach irritation, and low blood sugar. So whichever drink you choose, expect "somewhat better," not "fixed." There is no good evidence that Ultima, Liquid I.V., or any electrolyte drink prevents or shortens a hangover on its own.

### When Ultima might be the better hangover choice

There are a few situations where Ultima makes sense the morning after:

- **You have high blood pressure or have been told to limit salt.** A low-sodium drink plus food is a safer default than stacking salty mixes. Ask your doctor what's right for you.
- **You're managing diabetes.** You may prefer zero sugar, though low blood sugar after drinking is a real risk for people on insulin or certain diabetes pills, so eat something and follow your care plan.
- **You're only mildly thirsty and plan to eat a salty breakfast.** Food brings plenty of sodium. In that case the drink's job is mostly to get water into you, and Ultima does that pleasantly.

### When neither is enough

If you've vomited several times or have watery diarrhea, a true oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte or DripDrop, sipped slowly, is a better match than either. Our [Liquid I.V. vs Pedialyte comparison](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-vs-pedialyte-for-hangover) explains why. If nausea is your main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what helps beyond fluids.

## Ultima vs Liquid I.V.: Sugar and Keto

This is where Ultima clearly wins on paper. It has zero sugar and close to zero calories. The original Liquid I.V. has about 11 g of sugar and around 45 calories per stick.

To put 11 g in context: that's a bit under three teaspoons of sugar. It's much less than a regular soda or a full bottle of a classic sports drink, and for most active, healthy adults one stick on a hangover morning is not a concern. It matters more if:

- You drink it every day as your default "water."
- You're following a strict ketogenic diet.
- You have diabetes or prediabetes and are counting carbs.

If you want Liquid I.V.'s sodium without the sugar, the Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free line is the middle ground. It keeps a similar sodium level and swaps sugar for allulose and other sweeteners. The trade-off is that without real glucose, it loses some of the absorption advantage described above. For everyday hydration that trade-off barely matters. For serious dehydration it does.

## Ultima vs Liquid I.V.: Sodium and Blood Pressure

Here Ultima is the gentler choice. Around 50 to 60 mg of sodium per serving is tiny. You'd get more from a slice of bread. Liquid I.V.'s roughly 500 mg is a meaningful amount: US dietary guidelines advise most adults to stay under about 2,300 mg of sodium a day, and the American Heart Association suggests an ideal of 1,500 mg for many adults, especially those with high blood pressure.

That doesn't make Liquid I.V. unhealthy. Sodium isn't bad in itself; it's essential, and you genuinely need more of it when you're sweating heavily or losing fluid. The problem is using a high-sodium drink as a daily habit when you aren't losing much fluid, on top of an already salty diet.

**A simple rule of thumb:**

- **Losing fluid (hangover, heat, workout, illness):** sodium is useful. Liquid I.V. fits.
- **Not losing much fluid, just want flavored water:** sodium isn't needed. Ultima fits.

If you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, or you've been told to limit salt or fluids, ask your doctor before using either regularly.

## Potassium and Magnesium: Ultima's Strong Suit

Ultima's formula puts more weight on potassium and magnesium relative to sodium. Both minerals do real work. Potassium helps regulate heart rhythm, muscle function, and blood pressure, and most adults eat less of it than recommended. Magnesium is involved in hundreds of chemical reactions in the body, including muscle and nerve function, and heavy drinking over time is known to lower magnesium levels.

That makes Ultima a reasonable everyday drink for people who want a bit more of these minerals. A few cautions, though:

- **Liquid I.V. actually has more potassium per stick** than Ultima's standard formula, so "more potassium" isn't an automatic Ultima win. The difference is that Ultima pairs its potassium with magnesium and very little sodium.
- **Kidney disease and certain medicines change the picture.** Healthy kidneys clear extra potassium easily. People with kidney disease, or who take medicines that raise potassium (some blood pressure pills such as ACE inhibitors and ARBs, potassium-sparing water pills like spironolactone, and others), can build up too much. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using any potassium-containing drink mix regularly.
- **Magnesium supplements and the gut.** A single serving is fine for most people. Several servings, especially when your stomach is already upset from drinking, can contribute to loose stools.

## How to Use Either One After Drinking

The drink you choose matters less than how you use it. A simple routine:

1. **Before bed:** one serving plus a glass of plain water. Starting the night with some fluid on board helps with the thirst and dry mouth in the morning. Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing in more detail.
2. **On waking:** a glass of water, then one serving of your electrolyte drink over the next hour.
3. **Sip, don't chug.** If your stomach is unsettled, small mouthfuls every few minutes stay down better than a big glass at once.
4. **Eat when you can.** Food brings sodium, potassium, and carbohydrates on its own. Eggs, toast, bananas, broth, or a salty breakfast all help. See our [hangover breakfast guide](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) for ideas.
5. **Don't stack servings.** One or two servings over a hangover morning is plenty for most people. More isn't better.

### A note on the "special" versions

- **Liquid I.V. Energy** contains caffeine. A little caffeine can ease a caffeine-withdrawal headache, but it can also worsen nausea, a racing heart, and anxiety, which are already common after heavy drinking. Don't mix caffeine with alcohol on the night itself, since it can make you feel less drunk than you are.
- **Liquid I.V. Sleep** contains melatonin and other sleep ingredients. Don't take it with alcohol still in your system. Alcohol is already a sedative, and stacking sleep aids on top of it isn't a good idea. See our guide on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) for details.
- **Ultima** is mostly sold as a straightforward electrolyte mix, so this issue comes up less. Some newer Ultima products add other ingredients, so read the label of whatever version you buy.

## Is Ultima as Good as Liquid I.V.?

It depends entirely on the job. As a rehydration drink after real fluid loss, no: Liquid I.V. is better designed for that, and a medical ORS is better still. As an everyday, sugar-free, low-sodium way to make water more appealing and add some magnesium and potassium, Ultima is arguably the better product, and Liquid I.V. would be overkill.

A lot of people end up keeping both: Ultima for daily sipping, Liquid I.V. (or an ORS) in the cupboard for hangovers, travel, hot days, and stomach bugs. That's a sensible approach and costs less than it sounds, since you'd use the higher-sodium mix only occasionally.

## How Ultima and Liquid I.V. Compare With Other Popular Mixes

A few quick comparisons to help place both brands:

- **Ultima vs LMNT:** these sit at opposite ends of the sodium scale. LMNT has around 1,000 mg of sodium per stick, about twice Liquid I.V. and many times Ultima. Both are sugar-free. LMNT suits heavy sweaters and low-carb athletes; Ultima suits people who want minimal sodium. Our [LMNT vs Liquid I.V. comparison](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv) covers LMNT in more depth.
- **Ultima vs Nuun:** Nuun tablets are also low in sugar and moderate in sodium, landing somewhere between Ultima and Liquid I.V. See [Nuun vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/nuun-vs-liquid-iv).
- **Ultima vs Pedialyte:** Pedialyte is a true oral rehydration solution with much more sodium and some glucose. For a stomach bug or a rough hangover with vomiting, Pedialyte is the better tool.
- **Homemade:** a pinch of salt, a splash of juice, and water gets you surprisingly close to a basic rehydration drink for pennies. Our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) recipe shows how.

Our wider [electrolyte drinks compared guide](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) puts all the main options side by side, and our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains which minerals drinking actually depletes.

## Price and Convenience

Prices change too often to quote reliably, and both brands sell in packs of different sizes, so compare cost per serving at the store you use. In general, both are premium products compared with a sports drink or a homemade mix. Ultima's large tubs usually bring the per-serving price down for daily users. Liquid I.V. is often discounted in larger boxes at warehouse clubs.

Both come in single-serving stick packs that are easy to toss in a bag for travel or a night out. Both mix easily in a standard water bottle, though Ultima's light flavor can taste a little thin if you add more water than the label suggests.

## Who Should Be Careful With Either

Electrolyte drinks are safe for most healthy adults at the labeled dose. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you:

- Have high blood pressure, heart failure, or have been told to limit salt (more relevant for Liquid I.V.).
- Have kidney disease of any stage (relevant for both, because of sodium, potassium, magnesium, and phosphate).
- Take medicines that affect potassium or sodium, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, water pills, or lithium.
- Have diabetes and are counting carbohydrates (more relevant for original Liquid I.V.).
- Are pregnant, or are giving these to a child (pediatric dehydration has its own guidance, and a pediatric ORS is usually the better choice).

## When a Hangover Needs More Than a Drink Mix

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless, and they clear within a day. See a doctor or get urgent care if:

- You can't keep fluids down for several hours
- You're vomiting repeatedly, or you see blood in vomit or stool
- You've barely urinated in 8 hours or more, or your urine is very dark
- You feel faint, confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle
- Symptoms are getting worse instead of better by the afternoon

If someone who drank heavily is confused, hard to wake, having seizures, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, that may be [alcohol poisoning](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs), not a hangover. Call 911 right away and don't leave them alone. No drink mix is a substitute for emergency care.

And if you notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart that start when you *stop* drinking after several days of heavy use, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than trying to manage it with drinks or supplements.

## What About DHM?

Electrolyte drinks address fluid loss. They don't do anything about alcohol itself or the by-products your body makes when it breaks alcohol down. That's where some people add a DHM supplement. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal studies suggest it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde and may affect how alcohol acts on the brain, and human data are still limited. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't replace water, food, sleep, or simply drinking less.

If you want to try it, take it with plenty of water on the night you drink, alongside whichever electrolyte mix suits you. Popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [best DHM supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-dhm-supplements) compares the main brands.

The habits with the best evidence are still the boring ones: pace yourself, alternate alcohol with water, eat before and while you drink, and get a full night's sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers them in detail.

## The Bottom Line

- **Liquid I.V.** is a sodium-plus-sugar hydration mix built on oral rehydration science. It's the better pick after real fluid loss: a hangover, heat, travel, or a long workout.
- **Ultima** is a zero-sugar, low-sodium mix with potassium and magnesium. It's the better pick for everyday sipping, keto, or anyone limiting salt.
- Per serving, Liquid I.V. has roughly ten times Ultima's sodium. That one difference explains most of the comparison.
- Neither cures a hangover. They help with dehydration, which is real but usually not the main reason you feel bad.
- Talk to a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart disease, diabetes, or take medicines that affect sodium or potassium.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Ultima better than Liquid I.V.?**

It depends on the job. Liquid I.V. is better for real dehydration because it has about ten times the sodium plus a little glucose, which helps your body absorb and hold water. Ultima is better for everyday sipping if you want zero sugar and very little salt. Many people keep Ultima for daily use and Liquid I.V. or an oral rehydration solution for hangovers, heat, and illness.

**Which is better for a hangover, Ultima or Liquid I.V.?**

For most people, Liquid I.V. Alcohol makes you lose fluid and some sodium, and Liquid I.V. is designed to replace both. Ultima adds very little sodium, so it helps about as much as plain water. Ultima can make sense if you have been told to limit salt. Neither cures a hangover, and if you are vomiting or have diarrhea, a true oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte is a better choice.

**Does Ultima have sugar?**

No. Standard Ultima Replenisher has zero sugar and close to zero calories. It is sweetened with stevia leaf extract. Original Liquid I.V. has around 11 g of sugar per stick, while the Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free line swaps sugar for allulose and other sweeteners.

**How much sodium is in Ultima compared with Liquid I.V.?**

Ultima's standard formula has only around 50 to 60 mg of sodium per serving, while original Liquid I.V. has around 500 mg per stick. Both are mixed into about 16 ounces of water, so Liquid I.V. is roughly ten times saltier. Figures change between versions, so check your package.

**Is Ultima good for keto?**

Yes. With no sugar, close to zero calories, and a stevia sweetener, Ultima fits a ketogenic or low-carb diet. Because it is low in sodium, people on keto who sweat a lot may still need more salt from food or a higher-sodium sugar-free mix.

**Can I drink Ultima or Liquid I.V. every day?**

Most healthy adults can have Ultima daily without issue, and one Liquid I.V. a day is fine for many people, though daily use adds a meaningful amount of sodium and sugar. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or take medicines that affect sodium or potassium, ask your doctor before using either regularly.

**Can Ultima cause diarrhea?**

One serving is unlikely to cause problems for most people. Ultima contains magnesium, and larger amounts of magnesium can loosen stools. If alcohol has already upset your gut, drinking several servings at once could make diarrhea worse, so stick to one or two and sip slowly.
